tldr: When post-training large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models with real-world online reinforcement learning, researchers face two major hurdles: policy drift caused by unreliable value signals, and severe computational/communication overhead. This paper solves both using an algorithm that coordinates across two timescales (ACoB) and a state lifecycle management system (ACoB-Stream), achieving an ultra-high 98.3% task success rate with an average of just 45.8 minutes of real-world training.
hero_caption: The two-stage post-training pipeline of VLA-Precision. In Stage I, full-parameter imitation learning on human demonstrations produces an initial policy. In Stage II, an asynchronous actor-learner online RL setup autonomously refines the policy on real robots by co-bootstrapping intervention imitation and value estimation.
overview:
Recently, large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that integrate vision, language, and action to control robots have gained tremendous attention. While pre-training grants them the flexibility to handle a broad range of tasks, conventional imitation learning (behavioral cloning, or BC) tends to fail in tasks demanding millimeter precision and high repeatability—such as chemistry experiments—because small errors accumulate over time.

Real-world online reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising way forward by letting robots improve through autonomous trial and error. However, running online RL on massive VLA models on physical hardware poses two steep bottlenecks. The first is algorithmic stability: early on, inaccurate value estimates from the critic often cause "policy drift," eroding the model's pre-trained competence. The second is system efficiency: huge models demand massive compute and memory bandwidth, which introduces large synchronization lags between the robot and the learner, dragging the training loop down to an agonizing crawl.

To break through this dual bottleneck, the authors introduce "VLA-Precision." On the algorithmic side, they developed "ACoB," which couples rapid intervention-guided imitation with steady, long-term return and local preference-based value calibration across different timescales. On the system side, they built "ACoB-Stream," which eliminates redundant computation of invariant context and streams only the necessary data on demand.

Evaluated across nine high-precision real-world chemistry tasks, VLA-Precision achieved an exceptional 98.3% success rate with an average of only 45.8 minutes of online training per task, while boosting system throughput by up to 10.9$\times$ over baselines.
contributions: Proposed ACoB, an RL algorithm that links two timescales to achieve both rapid improvement via human intervention imitation and steady value calibration via local preferences and global returns, effectively preventing policy drift.

Developed ACoB-Stream, a system that decouples invariant states and streams data on demand, cutting compute, storage, and synchronization waste in large-VLA online RL to deliver up to a 10.9x throughput speedup.
Achieved a 98.3% success rate with an average of just 45.8 minutes of training across nine high-precision real-world chemistry tasks, spanning contact-rich insertions to bimanual coordination.

Designed an active isomorphic master teleoperation device featuring load-decoupled joint bearings and tiered torque sizing to collect high-precision demonstrations and enable seamless human interventions.

sections.heading: Why has real-world online RL been so difficult for VLAs?
sections.summary: While large VLA models generalize broadly, high-precision real-world tasks suffer from demo quality ceilings and compounding errors. Breaking through with real-world online RL encounters two major bottlenecks: policy drift from noisy value signals and massive computational overhead from model scale. This work tackles both.
sections.details:
VLA models pre-trained on large-scale multimodal datasets offer powerful flexibility, adapting to diverse environments from only a few demonstrations. However, in demanding settings like chemistry lab operations requiring millimeter or sub-millimeter precision and high repeatability, imitation learning (BC) alone falls short. Veering even slightly outside the demonstration distribution causes errors to snowball, leading to intermittent failures.

Breaking through this performance ceiling requires reinforcement learning (RL), where the robot explores through trial and error in the real world and learns action values from long-term returns. While RL in simulation is safe and easily parallelized, significant Sim-to-Real gaps in contact dynamics and visual rendering make direct transfer to high-precision physical tasks impractical.

Meanwhile, attempts to run online RL directly on physical hardware with VLAs run into two critical obstacles:

- Algorithmic Instability: Early in training, critic value estimates are noisy and inaccurate. Simply maximizing these imperfect Q-values causes "policy drift," destroying the desirable behaviors acquired during pre-training.
- System Efficiency Limits: Because large VLAs are enormous, the compute and memory-transfer costs of sampling from replay buffers and performing updates are massive. Synchronization between physical actors and the learner cannot keep up, causing learning throughput to plummet.

To tackle this dual challenge, the authors proposed "Asymmetric Co-Bootstrapping (ACoB)" as the algorithmic solution and "ACoB-Stream" as the system solution, bringing real-world online post-training of large VLAs firmly into practical territory.

sections.heading: Simulation, real-world RL, and the limits of existing systems
sections.summary: Prior work spans simulation RL, real-world RL with small models, and applying RL to pre-trained VLAs. However, they all suffer from Sim-to-Real gaps, massive rollout requirements, or policy drift. This research is positioned to overcome each of these shortcomings.
sections.details:
This section organizes related prior research into lineages and contextualizes the paper's contributions.

### Simulation-Based VLA Post-Training
Parallel simulation enables fast and safe RL exploration, giving rise to methods like RIPT-VLA, VLA-RL, and SimpleVLA-RL. However, accurately simulating contact-rich physics and complex optical properties (such as transparent glassware and liquid behavior) remains extremely difficult, inevitably degrading reliability when deployed to the real world.

### Real-World Reinforcement Learning
Real-world RL has the distinct advantage of directly learning from actual sensor noise and real dynamics. Methods incorporating human interventions, like HIL-SERL, reach high success rates quickly but struggle with within-task generalization. Furthermore, attempts applying RL to VLAs like Octo (such as ConRFT and Robo-Dopamine) suffer from policy drift when directly maximizing Q-values, degrading prior knowledge. In addition, applying RL to large VLAs as in $\pi^{*}_{0.6}$ required over 1,000 real-world rollouts per task, suffering from very poor feedback efficiency.

### Systems for Online RL
Asynchronous actor-learner architectures are standard for small models, but when scaled to massive VLAs, heavy forward passes, memory exhaustion, and saturated communication bandwidth become catastrophic. Workarounds like RL Token or EXPO-FT train only lightweight auxiliary heads, but this hinders holistic capability gains across the entire model. This work preserves the full capability of the VLA while pushing dataflow and computation across the entire system to maximum efficiency.

sections.heading: A deep dive into the ACoB algorithm and ACoB-Stream architecture
sections.summary: The proposed approach consists of the ACoB algorithm, which harmonizes rapid imitation with progressive value calibration, and the ACoB-Stream system, which boosts throughput via invariant context reuse and differential synchronization. Paired with a high-precision teleoperation device and compliant impedance control, it forms a complete real-world learning loop.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation and Pipeline
Training proceeds in two stages. In Stage I, the full VLA is trained with imitation learning on human demonstrations (Full-Parameter IL) to construct a task-specific prior policy $\Theta_{\mathrm{IL}}$. In Stage II, the visual-language prefix encoder and the base parameters of the Action Expert are frozen, and only the LoRA parameters $\theta$ inside the Action Expert are updated via online RL in an asynchronous actor-learner architecture.

### III-B Training the Action Expert: The ACoB Algorithm
The core of ACoB lies in "Asymmetric Co-Bootstrapping," which coordinates two distinct timescales:

- Progressive Value Calibration: The critic uses a $K$-ensemble architecture separating value and advantage ($Q = V + A$). For fully executed trajectories, global returns are propagated via standard temporal difference (TD) learning. However, when a human intervenes and overrides the robot's proposed action, no transition data exists for that rejected proposal. To handle this, a local preference ranking loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rank}}$ is introduced, directly enforcing that the advantage of the human-corrected action exceeds that of the rejected proposal by a specified margin.
- Relative-Advantage Policy Improvement: Maximizing raw Q-values causes policy collapse due to early overestimation noise. Instead, ACoB estimates the relative advantage difference between the current action and the reference policy (the frozen Stage I policy) using the most pessimistic estimate across the critic ensemble, smoothly optimizing it via a margined softplus function. Combining this with a flow-matching BC loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BC}}$ to rapidly absorb human interventions and successful rollouts, along with a regularization loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ to prevent straying too far from the reference policy, completely suppresses policy drift.

### III-C System Infrastructure: ACoB-Stream
To keep the learning loop from clogging with large VLAs, ACoB-Stream optimizes the data lifecycle across four stages:

- Context Generation: Because the frozen prefix KV cache does not change across updates, inference caches from the actor are retained and reused rather than discarded, eliminating redundant prefix forward passes during updates.
- Context Retention: Caches are deduplicated and stored on disk, while sliding-window sampling matched to the Linux page cache capacity in CPU RAM prevents disk I/O bottlenecks.
- Context Access: Updating the critic requires next-step contexts, whereas policy updates require both current- and next-step contexts. Targeted context IDs are prefetched and batched to the GPU on demand.
- Policy Synchronization: Instead of transmitting the entire VLA, only the updated Action Expert LoRA parameters are streamed to the actor and swapped atomically, minimizing synchronization latency.

### III-D Hardware and Real-World Deployment
For the UR5e, the authors developed a custom active isomorphic master device featuring dual-bearing load decoupling (diverting link loads away from servos) and tiered torque distribution matching gravity loads. A keyboard interface providing millimeter and sub-millimeter Cartesian nudging is also used for micro-alignment. On the robot side, force-controlled impedance control for the UR5e and torque-controlled impedance control for the Franka guarantee compliance, safety, and precision during contact.

captions.F3: The system architecture of ACoB-Stream. It resolves communication and compute bottlenecks between actor and learner by managing a four-stage context lifecycle: generation, disk retention, goal-specific prefetch access, and lightweight synchronization of trainable parameters only.

High-torque servos are placed at the base and low-inertia servos at the wrist, with specialized joint bearing structures diverting external loads away from servos to achieve high durability and smooth tracking.

sections.heading: Unprecedented success rates and high training throughput in chemistry tasks
sections.summary: Evaluated across four robot setups and nine precision chemistry tasks, VLA-Precision achieved a 98.3% success rate in an average of just 45.8 minutes of online training, vastly outperforming existing RL and VLA baselines. ACoB-Stream also demonstrated up to a 10.9x throughput improvement.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Tasks
Four physical setups were evaluated: UR5e (single-arm parallel gripper, multi-finger dexterous hand, and bimanual) and a Franka Research 3. The benchmark includes nine demanding chemistry laboratory tasks, each evaluated with randomized object positions and initial arm poses to test generalization:

- Contact-Rich (millimeter-level insertions): Cuvette Transfer, 2 mL Vial Transfer, Tube Rack Loading
- Contact-Light (flexible or slippery objects): Rubber Stopper Insertion, Alcohol Lamp Extinguishing, Pipette Tip Attachment
- Contact-Free (vision-guided precision dispensing): Bulb Dropper Transfer, Pipette Transfer and Ejection
- Bimanual Coordination: Tube Brushing

### Overall Performance and Learning Efficiency
Baselines included real-world RL methods (HIL-SERL, ConRFT, Robo-Dopamine) and fine-tuned imitation VLAs ($\pi_{0}$, $\pi_{0.5}$).

VLA-Precision achieved an average 98.3% success rate across all tasks (177/180 successful trials, reaching 100% on seven tasks) in an average of only 45.8 minutes of online learning per task. This outstripped the strongest RL baseline, Robo-Dopamine (which peaked at 10.0%), by 88.3 percentage points. It also improved upon standalone $\pi_{0.5}$ imitation learning (67.8%) by 30.5 percentage points, proving that online RL successfully broke through demonstration ceilings. Episode execution was also notably fast, averaging 27.6 seconds.

### System Efficiency of ACoB-Stream
ACoB-Stream was compared against configurations without KV cache reuse (No KV Cache), random sampling across full history (Disk Full Random), unoptimized context retrieval (Naive Context Access), and dynamic CPU RAM caching. The full ACoB-Stream executed 15,666 update cycles within 150 minutes, delivering a 10.95$\times$ throughput speedup and a 90.9% latency reduction compared to No KV Cache. Furthermore, by leveraging the Linux page cache via sliding-window sampling, it suffered zero I/O degradation even during extended training runs.

### Ablation Studies on the ACoB Algorithm
Ablations removing key components across four tasks revealed their critical roles:

- Without critic local preference (w/o critic preference): Overestimation of poor robot actions overridden by interventions went uncorrected, dropping success rates from 96.25% down to 26.25%.
- Without actor imitation (w/o actor BC): Intervention feedback could not be rapidly incorporated, dropping success to 20.00%.
- Without relative advantage / with absolute Q-maximization (w/o relative advantage): The policy fell prey to noisy value overestimation, collapsing success down to 8.75% while nearly tripling human interventions.

sections.heading: Keys to successful real-world VLA RL and future horizons
sections.summary: The success of this work stems from an asymmetric learning loop that preserves pre-trained knowledge alongside dedicated state lifecycle management. Key future directions include scaling to multi-stage, long-horizon bimanual manipulation and expanding to multi-task VLA-RL.
sections.details:
This section synthesizes key insights and highlights promising avenues for future research.

### Fundamental Driver of Success
The root bottleneck in real-world large-VLA RL was temporal asymmetry. While pre-training and imitation provide an initial policy that can already act reasonably well, the critic cannot provide reliable values until substantial online experience accumulates. Rushing to maximize raw Q-values across this gap causes policy collapse. ACoB embraces this asymmetry: it rapidly bootstraps high-quality experience through imitation while steadily calibrating the critic via relative advantages and local preferences, creating a virtuous learning cycle.

### Long-Horizon Bimanual Tasks and Action Representations
When extending to longer action sequences, end-effector delta action parameterization becomes paramount. While this paper adopted step-wise deltas relative to the immediately preceding step with a short execution horizon ($H_e=3$) for agile micro-corrections, extending the horizon compounds prediction errors (increasing $H_e$ from 3 to 6 dropped autonomous success from 58.3% to 6.7%). For long-horizon tasks, transitioning to chunk-wise deltas referenced to the start of the horizon appears promising.

### Scaling to Multi-Task Learning
Currently, separate LoRA parameters are trained per task. Extending the ACoB framework to concurrent multi-task online RL on a unified VLA model could enable cross-task experience sharing and further reduce data collection burdens.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.summary: By unifying the ACoB algorithm with the ACoB-Stream architecture, VLA-Precision dramatically accelerates and stabilizes real-world online RL for large VLAs. This represents a major leap toward autonomous skill acquisition in ultra-precise robotic domains like laboratory chemistry.
sections.details:
This work introduced VLA-Precision, an efficient framework for real-world online reinforcement learning of large Vision-Language-Action models.

- Algorithmically, ACoB couples fast human-intervention imitation with progressive value calibration from global returns and local preferences across timescales, completely suppressing policy drift while breaking through demonstration performance barriers.
- System-wise, ACoB-Stream establishes invariant-state decoupling and on-demand streaming principles, eliminating compute, memory, and sync bottlenecks to deliver up to a 10.9$\times$ throughput boost.
- In physical experiments across nine high-precision chemistry tasks and four robot embodiments, it achieved an outstanding 98.3% success rate with an average of just 45.8 minutes of online training per task.

These results establish a robust algorithmic and architectural standard for real-world online RL post-training of large VLAs, which previously struggled with computational costs and training instabilities.

takeaways: In online RL for large VLAs, optimizing raw Q-values causes policy drift due to early overestimation noise; optimizing relative advantage margins against a reference policy effectively preserves stability.

When a human overrides robot actions, the rejected proposal lacks a subsequent state transition; calibrating the critic directly with a local preference ranking loss rather than standard TD loss yields dramatic benefits.
Decoupling and reusing the large frozen prefix KV cache across episodes cuts compute and memory waste, boosting physical RL throughput by nearly an order of magnitude.

A two-stage paradigm—establishing baseline behavior via imitation learning (BC) and autonomously mastering millimeter-level contact alignments via online RL—is a winning recipe for high-precision robotic tasks.
limitations: The current implementation trains separate LoRA parameters per task, without yet achieving multi-task online RL where experience across multiple tasks continuously feeds into a single shared VLA.

Using step-wise delta actions requires maintaining short execution horizons ($H_e=3$) to prevent error accumulation; scaling to ultra-long-horizon complex manipulation will require rethinking the action representation.

A moderate amount of skilled human teleoperation intervention is still needed during early training to ensure safety and provide local preference data, meaning it is not yet fully unassisted or unattended learning.
